As oncology consistently dominates biotech deal-making activity , accounting for a significant portion of both deal volume and value, large pharmaceutical companies are continuously seeking to bolster their own pipelines with promising cancer assets developed by promising biotech innovators. In this article, we look at eight of the biggest oncology deals that have been made so far in 2026. Table of contents Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics AbbVie and RemeGen BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Roche and C4 Therapeutics Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS. The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs. Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion. Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines. The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.” The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The agreement also grants Eli Lilly an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the programs worldwide outside Greater China, while Innovent retains rights in Greater China. AbbVie and RemeGen Back to Top At the start of the year, AbbVie entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with RemeGen for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of RC148, a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-targeted bispecific antibody, which is currently being developed by RemeGen as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across multiple advanced solid tumors. PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs. In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer. Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory. BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis. Through its “three-in-one” synergistic mechanism of action, the asset is expected to enhance therapeutic efficacy, achieve tumor-specific drug distribution, and reduce treatment-related adverse effects. Positive preclinical results for it were presented at the 2025 Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) in Chicago, in the U.S. Under the agreement, Huahui Health received an upfront payment of $20 million. Additionally, the Chinese biotech is entitled to receive an additional $100 million option exercise payment and is eligible to receive up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Back to Top February 2026 saw Japanese big pharma Astellas enter into a global strategic collaboration with Vir Biotechnology to advance VIR-5500, a PRO-XTEN dual-masked CD3 T-cell engager targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) for the treatment of prostate cancer. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership. Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%. VIR-5500 is currently in phase 1 of development for people with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. The candidate combines a bispecific PSMA and CD3-binding T-cell engager with the PRO-XTEN masking technology, which is designed to keep the T-cell engagers masked (or inactive) until they reach the tumor microenvironment, reducing off-target effects and improving the therapeutic index. The financial terms of the agreement stated that Vir Biotechnology would receive $335 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments, would split U.S. profit/loss equally with Astellas (50/50), and would be eligible to receive up to an additional $1.37 billion in development, regulatory, and sales milestones, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on ex-U.S. net sales. Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Back to Top In February, Gilead Sciences stepped deeper into synthetic lethality by licensing a methionine adenosyltransferase 2a (MAT2A) inhibitor from China-based Genhouse Bio. At the time of the deal, the asset, dubbed GH31, was being developed by Genhouse for various tumor types and had already been given the green light from Chinese and U.S. regulators to enter clinical trials. Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales. This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die. These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise. Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer. Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization. licensing
Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales.
This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die.

These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise.

Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top
In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer.

degrader-antibody conjugate modality
Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization.
Meanwhile, the financial terms of the oncology deal stated that C4T would receive a $20 million upfront payment and, should Roche exercise its option for a third target, C4T would receive an additional payment. C4T is also eligible to receive more than $1 billion in discovery, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments and is entitled to tiered royalties on future sales, subject to reductions under certain circumstances as described in the agreement.
